newsitem.title: USA: Bob Dole busy actor, writer in post-election life.
newsitem.headline: Bob Dole busy actor, writer in post-election life.

text.p: Nearly five months after losing his race for the U.S. presidency, Bob Dole keeps busy acting, writing and accepting honours as he searches for the perfect niche in a world outside politics.
"One thing he won't be doing is jumping out of planes," said Dole aide Clarkson Hine, referring to ex-President George Bush's much-publicised parachute jump in Arizona on Tuesday.
But Dole, 73, clearly admired the 72-year-old Bush's sky-diving fling.
He wrote a congratulatory note to Bush -- his victorious rival for the 1988 Republican White House nomination -- who was commemorating his wartime bail-out from a crippled plane.
A former Senate Republican leader who spent 35 years in Congress before challenging President Bill Clinton in last year's election, Dole has said little publicly about any future occupational plans.
One project surfaced last week when he agreed to lead a drive to raise $100 million for a World War II Memorial on Washington's central Mall near the White House.
This is a chore dear to his heart.
Some 52 years ago a German shell nearly killed the young lieutenant Dole on the front in Italy, shattering his right shoulder and rendering his right arm permanently useless.

He betrays no bitterness over the physical and emotional scars that left him. But it has made him sensitive to the needs of the disabled and a leader in support of federal medical insurance for the handicapped and elderly, a subject he recently addressed in a Washington Post op-ed piece.

Dole is also in some demand as a celebrity wit hamming it up on television talk and comedy shows such as NBC's "Saturday Night Live" and "The Tonight Show" with Jay Leno and CBS's "Late Show" with David Letterman, among others.

One comedy turn came at the White House in January when Clinton honoured Dole's many years of public service by bestowing the Presidential Medal of Freedom -- America's highest civilian honour -- in a moving ceremony.
Dole began his acceptance remarks with the familiar opening of the presidential inaugural oath -- "I Robert Joseph Dole ..." then added, as the audience roared with laughter, "Sorry, wrong speech."
"I had a dream that I would be here this historic week receiving something from the president -- but I thought it would be the front-door key."
Last week, he wrote Clinton a tongue-in cheek note after the president's surgery for a torn knee tendon.

He recalled that he had taken a famous tumble himself during the campaign -- off a stage in front of cameras -- and added: "Should you need someone to fill in and run the country during your recovery, give me a call."
While he seeks the right role away from elective office, Dole has also signed with two booking agents for speeches and endorsements and is considering writing a book, aides say.
One of the endorsements was a humorous television commercial for a credit card company shown to millions of viewers during the Super Bowl football championship.

He also did a public service television spot to promote early detection of prostate cancer through a simple blood test that can detect possible cancer. Dole himself is a survivor of prostate cancer surgery.
He also plans to rejoin the national political dialogue.
One example was a New York Times op-ed piece published Thursday, promoting a plan he pushed in the Senate to make broadcasters pay for licenses for digital television.
He chastised the Clinton administration and Congress for planning to give away a new spectrum he said could be sold for up to $70 billion to help balance the federal budget.
While Dole remains without a full-time job, his wife Elizabeth has a high-profile one as president of the American Red Cross, a job she held before the campaign.
